title: Three Reasons You Shouldn't Use Your Browser's Password Manager (and What to Use Instead)
body:
Built-in tools have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 4, 2026
            
            
                        Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    
        
        Most modern browsers have built-in password management, allowing you to save your credentials and automatically fill them when logging into your accounts on various websites. And while Google Password Manager on Chrome and similar tools in other browsers like Firefox, Brave, and Microsoft Edge certainly simplify the process of storing and using stronger passwords, they have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality. Here's why you should use a dedicated password manager instead.Browser password managers only work within the browserIf you store your passwords in your browser, it can fill your credentials on websites within the browser itself. (If you're an Android user, Google Password Manager also syncs to your device and works across any browser or app.) But if you use multiple browsers or want to log into apps on your iPhone or PC, you'll have to manually copy and paste your password from the browser into those form fields—not ideal, from a standpoint of both convenience and security. Browser password managers are more vulnerable to security risksBrowser password management is, on a basic level, secure: Google uses the same AES encryption in transit and at rest that many dedicated password managers do, and allows it you to add biometric authentication for auto-filling credentials. However, they're not zero-knowledge by default: Google manages your encryption key unless you enable on-device encryption so that your vault can only be unlocked on your device, by you, with your Google password or biometrics. Firefox also uses AES-256 encryption and has a "primary password" feature to protect your stored data, without which anyone who has access to your computer or browser profile can view your saved passwords. It's on the user to add these layers of security, as they're not on by default.As Wired points out, the more serious problem isn't encryption, but rather the risk inherent in storing passwords in a high-value account that could be targeted—either by someone who gains access to your device or as part of a takeover attempt, such as a phishing or credential stuffing attack. This creates a single point of failure, and if someone gets into your Google account or your browser of choice, your passwords for everything else are also compromised. Browser password managers have only basic featuresBrowser password managers do basically one thing, which is store your login credentials and fill them in on websites when you visit them in the browser. Google Password Manager will also alert you if your password has been compromised in a breach, but most browsers lack any additional tools and features, such as password customization, secure sharing, email masking, emergency access, and storage for payment cards, identity data, and documents. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use a dedicated third-party password manager insteadThe solution is to opt for a dedicated password manager that works across platforms and devices and offers a layer of protection outside of your browser. There are many excellent password managers to choose from, including free services like Bitwarden and privacy-focused Proton Pass (which also has a decent free tier). The best password managers also have features like secure file storage, encrypted credential sharing, and data breach monitoring, making them useful tools in your privacy and security arsenal. Of course, even a browser password manager is better than nothing at all, if the alternative is to reuse the same easy-to-remember credentials across your accounts. (It's also likely your reused passwords don't meet basic security standards and can be easily guessed.) Password storage in Chrome, Firefox, and other browsers do reduce the friction of shifting to strong, unique passwords for your accounts, and that alone is a solid step. But a third-party password manager is a superior choice if you're willing to invest a bit of time and energy into setting it up. 
            
                        
                
                    
                                            
                
                
                                            
    More by Emily

title: TikTok Just Announced These Four New Features for Comments
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: NurPhoto / Contributor via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            TikTok announced four new features coming to its comment section over the next month.
                                            Next month, the app will roll out voice comments, which will let users record and post audio up to 60 seconds.
                                            Creators can add polls to their comment sections to invite viewers to vote on up to five options at a time.
                                            Finally, TikTok is rolling out photo carousel and Live Photos comments as well.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        TikTok is famous for its addictive algorithm. And while the videos are certainly the app's main focus, I find the most entertainment in the comments. TikTok commenters can be hilarious, especially since they can use both text and photos to make their jokes. Social media comments are often vile, and while TikTok isn't immune to trolls and their ilk, its comments are generally something else. Now, the comments are changing. On Thursday, TikTok announced four new features that will make comments more visual, interactive, and, well, loud. Not all of these features are out quite yet, but by next month, you might not recognize TikTok's comment section. Text and photo comments aren't going anywhere, but you may find that the comment section is about to get a bit louder. Starting next month, TikTok will support voice comments up to 60 seconds long, which adds a wholly unique type of comment to the mix. Based on TikTok's press release, you can still attach a text-based comment to your voice comment, similar to how photo comments work.While friends may post voice comments on each other's videos à la voice memos in a group chat, I'm guessing that commenters in general will use this feature in ways TikTok doesn't necessarily intend. In fact, this may birth a new type of meme, where users spam videos with obnoxious sound effects and reaction sounds. Think the sounds added to meme edits of viral videos, but in comment form. It's going to be messy, and, likely, hysterical.   
Starting this week, you may see a new interactive element to TikTok comments: polls. TikTok says creators can add polls to the comments of their videos, with up to five voting options per poll. Rather than ask for opinions in the comments, creators can use a poll instead. Creators can choose how long voting lasts, and watch votes appear in real time. It's a small change, but one that could be useful to both big and small creators looking for input from their viewers. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You're no longer limited to posting static images in TikTok's comments. TikTok now supports uploading Live Photos to comments, which should also prove interesting. I could see people thinking they're posting a standard image, but accidentally uploading a Live Photo instead. But seeing as users already know how to add GIFs to comments, I'm not sure how many will want to upload Live Photos. This one might be reserved more for friends commenting on friends' videos, but we'll have to see how users react to know for sure. This last update is perhaps a bit more useful than Live Photo comments. TikTok says it's working on allowing users to upload up to nine photos in one comment, which means the comments section may be literally full of pictures once this launches en masse.  Like standard carousels, users will be able to swipe through your photo uploads, including in a full-screen view. This one will roll out over the course of this month.

This makes Labor Day one of the best times of year to buy tools. DeWalt tools are known for being durable and reliable, and they’re on sale right now at Lowe’s for Labor Day. Here are some of the best deals I've found.Best deals on cutting and shaping toolsCordless cutting tools can be better than their corded counterparts for getting into tight spaces—and they’re more portable, too. Here are a couple of the best deals on DeWalt cutting and shaping tools on sale at Lowe’s for Labor Day.The DeWalt 12-volt oscillating multitool is on sale for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a wood-cutting blade, a multimaterial blade, and a sanding adapter. It doesn’t come with a battery or a charger, so you’ll need a DeWalt 12-volt battery and charger to use it. This tool can cut wood, metal, PVC, drywall, and tile and you can use the adapter to use it as a sander that will work in tight spaces.The DeWalt 12-volt, 5 ⅜-inch circular saw is on sale for $99, 41% off its usual price. A powered driver can make assembling shelves or taking apart your HVAC panel much easier. Here are a couple of the best Labor Day deals on DeWalt powered drivers at Lowe’s.The DeWalt ⅜-inch cordless powered ratchet is on sale for $99, 50% off its typical price. title: 10 Hacks Every Proton Mail User Should Know
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Zain bin Awais/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Proton Mail is a privacy-focused mail service that strips trackers from messages, maintains zero-access encryption (meaning Proton can't read or hand over the content of your emails), and offers end-to-end encryption between Proton mailboxes. If you're a Proton user, there are a handful of other hacks you should know to maximize these privacy features and make sending and receiving emails as seamless as possible. Proton Mail is free to use if you have just one email address, but storage is limited to just 500 MB, which will fill up fast if you are receiving messages with large attachments. You can upgrade to a Plus subscription for $4 per month to get 15 GB of storage—the same amount available to most Google users—but if you don't want to pay anything, you can at least double your limit to 1 GB by completing Proton's onboarding process within 18 days of signing up. Look for a Get more storage option on the left sidebar of your mailbox, and click an action to complete the task. Once you've finished the checklist, you'll unlock an additional 500 MB of storage on your account. Reserve an email address for your child in their nameIf you have a relatively common name, it's likely that many email addresses using simple conventions, such as firstname.lastname, have already been claimed. By the time your kids are old enough to set up their own accounts, pickings may be even slimmer. You can go ahead and reserve a username through Proton Mail for them, and they have 15 years to activate it. Once they're old enough, they'll already have a private email set up. Choose an address and pay $1 toward the Proton Foundation, then save the voucher to share with your child down the line. 
Use Easy Switch to migrate external email addressesIf you're moving to Proton Mail from a different email provider or simply want all of your messages in one inbox, you can use Proton's Easy Switch feature to connect with and import from Gmail, Yahoo Mail, Outlook, and any other provider that allows IMAP access. Once Easy Switch is on, you'll be able to receive and send messages from your external address within Proton, and any mail sent to another Proton user from that address will be end-to-end encrypted. You'll retain copies of messages in your external inbox, so you don't need to make the full transition immediately. Easy Switch can also migrate your contacts and calendars. Go to Settings > Import via Easy Switch, choose your email service, and follow the prompts. Customize the Undo Send timer to recall emailsWe've all sent emails we wish we could take back thanks to a typo we didn't notice, an attachment we forgot to add, or a message we regret. Proton Mail has a delayed send feature that gives you up to 20 seconds to change your mind before your email is out of your hands. The timer is set at 10 seconds by default, but you can adjust it down to 0 or 5 seconds or up to 20. Go to Settings > Messages and composing, scroll down to the Composing section, and choose your desired time from the Undo send dropdown.Create aliases to filter mail to specific foldersThere are plenty of good reasons to use an email alias, from keeping your primary address private to easily filtering messages from mailing lists. Proton Mail supports unlimited plus addressing, meaning you can simply add a plus symbol and word after your username to create a new email—such as [username][email protected]—and receive messages in your regular inbox (with filters if you set them up). This can be done when you sign up for an account or add your email to a list. Alternatively, you can create a randomly generated email alias, which keeps your username hidden. Free users get up to 10, while paid subscribers can create unlimited aliases. On the web interface, click the security shield icon, go to Hide-my-email aliases, and click New alias. Add a password to encrypt emails to non-Proton usersMessages between Proton users are automatically encrypted end to end, but if your recipient doesn't use Proton Mail, you can set up a password for your emails to keep them private. Replies to password-protected emails are also encrypted (though your reply to that reply will require you to re-enable encryption). When you compose your message, click the padlock icon in the bottom toolbar and enter a password and password hint. You can set an expiration date as well. Note that you'll need to share the password with the recipient separately.  
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Set expiration timers to automatically delete emails from recipients’ inboxesAnother Proton Mail security feature is the expiration timer, which will auto-delete emails you send and receive after a set period, preventing messages from hanging around in inboxes and sent folders indefinitely. Messages that you send to other Proton Mail users as well as password-protected emails to those outside of Proton can be set to expire. If you have a paid account, you can also set emails you receive to self-destruct (in addition to auto-delete for messages in trash). Click the hourglass icon at the bottom of the message and set the expiration date and time. If you are sending a password-protected email to a non-Proton user, check the box. Then hit Set. When you take a photo, image metadata may reveal locations, times and dates, and other information that can be used to track you if it falls into the wrong hands. Proton Mail can strip that out for sent images, so you can share photos via email without giving any unnecessary data away. When you attach an image to an email draft, choose Remove metadata when prompted. Turn on Message Content Search to build a local and searchable index of your emails Because of Proton's encryption, the standard search feature reads only names, dates, email addresses, and subject lines. If you want to include message content, you'll need to enable the feature that builds a local index in your browser, protecting it from intrusion unless someone has physical access to your device. Click the search bar at the top of your inbox on the web app and tap Enable next to Search message content. Click Enable to confirm. Note that indexing does require storage space, but once complete, it'll automatically update as long as your browser is open. Activate your short domain to get a shorter, simpler addressBy default, Proton Mail addresses end in @proton.me (unless you connect your own domain). But users on paid plans have the option to add a short domain, which is simply [username]@pm.me. You can send messages from either, and both route to your inbox. The shorter address is easier to remember and share, such as when you're giving our your email over the phone. To enable it, go to Settings > Identity and addresses. You must be a paid subscriber to activate a short domain address—if you downgrade to the free plan, you will still be able to receive (but not send) messages sent to your @pm.me address.

title: Here's What Lifehacker Readers Think Apple Will Announce on Wednesday
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 5, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jeffrey Hazelwood/Lifehacker
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        On Wednesday, Apple will finally host its big fall event, and we will likely get our first look at the Apple Watch Series 12, iPhone 18 Pro, and iPhone Ultra, Apple's first foldable iPhone. In the lead-up to this keynote, Lifehacker ran the third and final round of our Big Guessing Game, inviting readers to make predictions about what Apple will announce this week. While we won't know the answers to those questions until Apple officially confirms them during the event, here's a look at what readers think will happen. Question 1: Which product will Apple discuss first? 
The rumors strongly predict that Apple will announce new iPhones and a new Apple Watch on Wednesday, but there's always the possibility of more devices as well. Apple may release new AirPods—with or without embedded cameras—and while there's a chance they'll announce new Macs, I'm skeptical, given that Apple surprised us all with Mac news last week. My first question of the third round of the Big Guessing Game was about which of these products Apple would announce first. (To be clear, we posted the quiz before Apple's surprise Mac announcements.) The majority of respondents (49%) believe Apple will start with its iPhone news, while 23% believe the company will kick things off with Apple Watch. Smaller percentages believe Apple will focus on other products first: 16% think they'll announce new Macs first (sorry!), while 12% think AirPods will get the first shoutout. 
Question 2: Will former Apple CEO Tim Cook make an appearance?Wednesday's keynote will be Apple's first with a new CEO since the iPhone 4S event back in 2011. Tim Cook is no longer head of Apple; as such, new Apple CEO John Ternus will lead this week's event. That said, Apple events feature numerous employees throughout, and since Tim Cook is still Apple's executive chair, it stands to reason Cook could make an appearance on Wednesday. Lifehacker readers were pretty split on this question, though there was a clear majority. 55% of respondents think Cook will make an appearance, while 45% believe he will not. I could see the logic behind both: It might only make sense for Cook to "pass the baton" to Ternus, so to speak. On the other hand, Apple might want to establish the new "Ternus" era, and featuring Cook may muddy the waters.  Question 3: When will preorders for the foldable iPhone Ultra begin?The iPhone Ultra will likely steal the show on Wednesday. It'll be Apple's first foldable iPhone, will likely cost over $2,000, and will possibly be delayed. To that point, I asked Lifehacker readers when the iPhone Ultra's preorder will actually open up. Most are optimistic, with 43% responding that iPhone Ultra will be available to preorder this month. Another 33% think Apple will open up preorders in October, while 15% think the Ultra will be unavailable until November. A final 9% think Apple will open preorders in another month entirely. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Question 4: How long will Apple's keynote last?Apple events are rarely short. The company typically has a lot of announcements to get through, and even though these keynotes are now pre-recorded, they can run for as long as a feature-length movie. However, there's no set runtime for Apple events, which makes it a perfect guessing-game question. The majority (51%) of Lifehacker readers think that Apple's keynote will run 90 to 120 minutes long; 41% think that the event will be a bit shorter, running from 60 to 90 minutes; and a slim respondent pool (8%) thinks that Apple's event will be long, running more than two hours. I don't think that's likely, but it's not impossible—maybe Apple will go quite in-depth on that foldable iPhone. Question 5: Will new Apple CEO John Ternus bring back "One More Thing?"
"One more thing" was an Apple event staple for years, made famous by then-CEO Steve Jobs. The company would save a huge announcement for the end of the show and introduce it by saying "One more thing." It would be a fun nod for Ternus to bring back the slogan, but, again, perhaps the new CEO wants to carve his own path. Most Lifehacker readers think he'll do it, though: 61% think "One more thing" is coming back this year, compared to 39% who don't. Personally, I hope he does it, and I hope that whatever gets announced is actually surprising, and not something that's been leaked already.

title: I'm Obsessed With the 'Conversate' App on These Smart Glasses
body:
Stephen Johnson
                            
        
            Stephen Johnson
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceStephen Johnson is a senior staff writer at Lifehacker covering pop culture and technology, including the columns “The Out-of-Touch Adults’ Guide to Kid Culture” and “What People Are Getting Wrong This Week.”
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 4, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Stephen Johnson
                            
    
            
            
        
            We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.
        
    
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I am obsessed with the "Conversate" app in my Even Realities G2 smart glasses. Overall, the glasses are sci-fi cool—they project a small, monochrome HUD in front of your eyes but look like normal glasses—but Conversate is essential. The AI-driven productivity tool is designed for work meetings but it's fun in social settings too, and you can use it to scam free drinks from bartenders. Use Conversate and never take notes in a meeting againIf you've ever left a work meeting thinking, "wait, am I supposed to file the TPS reports, or is it Gary's week?" consider Conversate. I don't multi-task well, so listening while taking notes can be difficult. Conversate solves that problem.Here's how it works: You hit the start button on the app, and the AI listens and transcribes everything anyone says in real time. The text is just out of your eyesight unless you glance up at it, so it isn't distracting but if someone asks a factual question, you'll get a silent answer in a pop-up window in your glasses. If you share this fact, it can make you look very smart. Or like a know-it-all, so use wisely. If someone says a person's or a company's name, you get a pop-up that tells you who/what they are too. Usually this is useless (I already know what Google is and who Jesus Christ is), but occasionally, it gives needed context. 

    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
When the meeting is over, you can check out a summary of what was discussed, and Conversate will highlight anything that looks like a task for you. You can then take those tasks and migrate them to your glasses' to-do list with a click, so you have a checkable list of action items floating before your eyes whenever you want it. I realize that all of these functions could be done with a number of smart phone apps, but with Conversate, you keep your phone in your pocket—much more unobtrusive. How to use Conversate to win bar bets and fake being smartI used the last generation of Even Realities smart glasses to win a drink from a bartender, and Conversate makes this kind of skullduggery even easier. It's constantly listening for questions  and feeding you answers, so if you're a dishonest person, you can totally rule at trivia night, impress your friends with your human calculator skills, or tell everyone the day of the week they were born. An added trickery bonus: G2s don't look like smart glasses, and if you pair them with the ring controller, no one will ever know that you are cheating your way through life. How to have fun at parties with ConversateThis last use really depends on who you hang out with, but in the right crowd, Conversate becomes a hilarious party game. It's funny to read the AI's stilted definitions for common terms back to people, a beat behind the conversation. It's fun when your friends start saying obscure names to see whether your spectacles will tell you who they are. It's fun for people to invent "action items" that you will supposedly have to do later too. Everyone at the party will call you a nerd, but they will still want to try out your glasses. Are they secretly jealous of your cutting-edge techness? Probably not, to be honest. Anyway, when you are finished hanging out with your friends, Conversate will translate the party's banter and small talk into "corporate-speak" summaries, which I find delightful. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Later in your life, you can remember the barbecue you went to like this:Meeting Summary: : Retrospective on Social Logistics and Lifecycle Events1. Resource Management & Historical Social ModelsContext: Discussion regarding the evolution of "barbecue social gatherings."Key Point: Participants compared current hospitality standards to a legacy "Bring Your Own Meat" (BYOM) model.Outcome: The BYOM framework was noted for its ability to facilitate social gatherings with zero capital expenditure from the host.2. Asset Utility: Off-Road PlatformsContext: Review of 4-Wheel Drive (4WD) Jeep performance.Key Point: The group discussed the long-term viability and "fun" ROI of Jeep vehicles.Outcome: High consensus that the mobility benefits of 4WD systems outweigh the mechanical maintenance requirements.

    Table of Contents
    
        
        Back in 2004, I was cool enough to own a Motorola Razr when it was the trendiest phone around, so I’m excited to see it making a comeback more than 20 years later, even if I’m now an iPhone user. The release of the Motorola Razr+ taps into the nostalgia boom, reviving its iconic flip-phone design with a larger outer display and plenty of modern features, and right now, T-Mobile is offering a brand new device for free (no trade-in required) when you activate a new line on an eligible Experience Beyond plan.
In this case, “free” means getting the phone’s cost back in the form of monthly bill credits. The Razr+ normally costs $999.99, and this T-Mobile deal spreads that value across 36 monthly bill credits. Essentially, you’ll pay for the phone through your financing agreement and receive offsetting credits over three years. You’ll still have to pay sales tax on the pre-discount price at checkout, as well as T-Mobile’s $35 device connection charge.To qualify for the deal, new and existing customers can activate a new line on an Experience Beyond 2.0 account. (Existing customers who are still on the older Experience Beyond or Go5G Next plans may qualify as well.) The plan starts at $100 a month with AutoPay, before taxes and fees. The major perk here of this offer that there’s no trade-in requirement, making the deal more straightforward than many flagship phone promotions, especially if you don’t have another device to hand over.There are a couple of caveats to consider: The promotional line needs to stay active and in good standing if you want to keep getting those monthly credits. If you cancel the line or the whole account, those credits will stop, and you’ll need to pay the remaining phone balance. Additionally, if you pay the phone off early, the bill credits will end, too. According to T-Mobile, credits can take up to two billing cycles to appear, and customers who canceled their lines within the past three months might need to reactivate them before qualifying. You can get up to four discounted devices per account, but this deal can’t be combined with other promotions. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The Razr+ runs on the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8s Gen 3 processor and has a 4-inch external display that can run full apps, letting you respond to messages, navigate maps, and listen to music without opening the foldable. Ultimately, if you’ve been craving that flip phone nostalgia and are already committed to T-Mobile’s premium Experience Beyond plan, this is a great way to get your hands on a Motorola Razr+ without a trade-in. For other folks, the required plan cost and 36-month commitment are worth considering before you sign up.

title: I Tried Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google’s Latest AI Upgrade, and It (Mostly) Lives Up to the Hype
body:
David Nield
                            
        
            David Nield
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceDavid Nield is a technology journalist from Manchester in the U.K. who has been writing about gadgets and apps for more than 20 years. He has a bachelor's degree in English Literature from Durham University, where he also spent a term as editor of the award-winning student newspaper Palatinate. His journalism career started in print media, where he contributed to and edited several technology magazines and bookazines sold in the U.K. and internationally. More recently, he has worked as a freelancer for some of the biggest technology publications on the web, covering everything from on-the-ground reporting about product launches, to detailed explainers and how-to guides on apps, gadgets, and platforms. His expertise covers broad areas of consumer tech, including smartphones, laptops, wearables, and AI.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 3, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Google has new AI models to show off.
                                                    Credit: Google
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Gemini 3.8 Flash is now available to Pro and Ultra subscribers.
                                            The model is better at reasoning, coding, and complex tasks.
                                            There are noticeable improvements over the earlier Flash 3.6 model.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Google has rolled out two new AI models: Gemini 3.8 Flash (the "intelligent workhorse model" for everyday prompting), and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber (available to "trusted defenders" for cybersecurity protection). While we only got Gemini 3.7 a matter of weeks ago, the new model brings with it some substantial improvements.According to Google, reasoning and coding are better than ever with Gemini 3.8 Flash, and there are "significant" improvements across "software engineering, agentic tasks, and critical, multi-step reasoning in specialized domains"—so this is very much an update for advanced AI, rather than your basic prompting. You'll find Gemini 3.8 Flash available now inside the Gemini app if you use either the AI Pro plan ($19.99 a month) or the AI Ultra plan ($99.99 or $199.99 a month). There's nothing yet for users on the free tier or the $7.99-per-month AI Plus plan, though these models do trickle down to lower tiers over time, as upgrades are released.Gemini Flash is new and improvedYou'd be forgiven for being more than a little confused by all the Gemini AI models Google has pushed out in recent months. For some time now, the models have been split into Flash-Lite, Flash, and Pro, and as you go up that scale, the AI gets slower, more capable at deeper reasoning and complex queries, and more expensive. (Not to mention, these models have different thinking levels too).
With the Pro category, we're still on Gemini 3.1 Pro that launched in February 2026. While a follow-up was mentioned at Google I/O in May, it's yet to be made public. The Flash channel is moving along much more quickly, and it was only a few months ago in December that the first Gemini Flash 3.0 was previewed.
    
            
            Gemini 3.8 Flash is now available in Pro and Ultra.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
Now we have Gemini 3.8 Flash. As per Google's benchmarks (which you should always take with a pinch of salt), it offers improvements over its predecessor when tackling "long-horizon software engineering" (so full projects rather than small tools), knowledge work (synthesizing and digging into information), complex legal workflows, financial analysis, and agentic activities. Gemini 3.8 Flash is particularly good at complex engineering problems, Google says, and has improved in multi-step reasoning across science, math, humanities, and professional fields. It'll go into more depth to figure answers out, run more checks on their accuracy, and work better at combining different skills in one response.
    
            
            Google Maps, MS-DOS style, courtesy of Gemini 3.8 Flash.
                                        Credit: Google
                    
    
There are safety measures in place too: The AI has guardrails to block misuse concerning chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cyber offense lines of questioning, and is better than ever at resisting prompt injection attacks (where prompts are engineered to try and get the AI to do something malicious). It all looks impressive on the surface, as do the demos Google showcases here: One of them is a fully working version of Google Maps inside an MS-DOS interface, which will particularly appeal if (like me) you started using computers back in the days of the command prompt.Testing Gemini 3.8 Flash against Gemini 3.6 FlashWhile I don't have any long-horizon software projects on the go at the moment, I did put the new Gemini 3.8 Flash up against the Gemini 3.6 Flash model that's available to free users in a variety of tasks: designing an interactive Solar System animation, summarizing and simplifying a dense scientific paper, and analyzing the last week of emails in my Gmail account (one of the toughest engineering challenges I know).
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
To begin with, Gemini 3.8 Flash was noticeably faster: 23 seconds versus 27 seconds for building a space simulation, 15 seconds versus 20 seconds for the science summary, and more or less equal on the emails. Add up those percentages over huge projects and multiple tasks, and you can see that the new model really does get stuff done faster.
    
            
            The Solar System, as rendered by Gemini 3.6 Flash.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker/Gemini
                    
    

    
            
            The more realistic, detailed version, from Gemini 3.8 Flash.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker/Gemini
                    
    
For the Solar System test, the simulations were pretty similar—perhaps a sign of how fast they've progressed that a task like this is straightforward for them now. Gemini 3.8 Flash did do a slightly better job at the quality of the renderings though, as the planets look noticeably more "real." When it came to the science summary, again both AI models tackled a tricky problem well. If anything, Gemini 3.6 Flash presented a more understandable summary—perhaps as it's a simpler model—but I found the visualizations and diagrams presented by Gemini 3.8 Flash more helpful (remember the images are created by Nano Banana 2 in both cases, but the info is provided by the underlying model).
    
            
            All Gemini models use the same image generator, but pass it different information.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker/Gemini
                    
    

    
            
            I found the Gemini 3.8 Flash illustrations (bottom) easier to parse overall.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker/Gemini
                    
    
On the email challenge, there wasn't much to choose between them: Both accurately summarized what was in my inbox and picked out the same items that needed attention (emails that weren't that important as it happens, but that's a whole other story). This is still a job I prefer to do myself, but these AI models are getting more reliable.The speed and sophistication gains that Google has talked about are clearly there, even in small-scale tests like this—and it's notable that creating mini web apps and digging through complex physics papers are now straightforward for Flash models as well as the Pro equivalents, which is maybe something to think about if you're considering signing up for a Google AI plan. (Of course, if you want to upgrade to Gemini 3.8 Flash, you'll need to pay.)

title: Apple Just Made Its First Product Announcements of the Season
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        August 25, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Apple
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Ahead of its expected September keynote, Apple announced two new Mac upgrades—and issued some quiet updates on the side.
                                            Apple's Mac mini now comes in either M6 or M5 Pro, and is aimed at AI users who run agents on their Mac minis.
                                            The company's powerful Mac Studio line now comes in either M5 Max or M5 Ultra variants.
                                            In addition, Magic Keyboards now have a upgraded design to bring them in line with the company's latest MacBooks.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Anyone who follows Apple news knows the company has some big announcements on the horizon. While we don't know the exact date yet, Apple typically hosts a big fall keynote in September to announce brand new products—including the latest generation of iPhones. This year should prove especially monumental, as the world expects Apple to reveal its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Ultra. But while I expected to wait until next month to learn about Apple's newest devices, I was surprised to find Mac news on my feed Tuesday morning. Apple being Apple, the company made a few new announcements well ahead of its expected keynote, signaling both its enthusiasm for the Mac in this age of AI, but also that its fall event is likely going to be focused squarely on the iPhone. Here's what's new.If you like making predictions about what products and services Apple will announce this year, make sure to check out Lifehacker's Big Guessing Game, which is currently in its third round. The winner will win the latest Apple Watch.    
Apple's new Mac mini is more powerful (and expensive) than everThe star of the show today might just be the new Mac mini. Apple's tiny Mac has been all the rage lately, with users buying them up to power AI agents like OpenClaw. While the previous generation of Mac mini was getting harder to find, Apple's refreshed models might make them more accessible—so long as you're willing to pay the inflated price tag. At first glance, the new Mac mini looks the same as the previous Mac mini. Of course, the core upgrade is internal: Now, the Mac mini comes with one of two of Apple's M-series chips: the brand-new M6 and the existing, more powerful, M5 Pro. The M6 chip has a 12-core GPU (two more cores than the previous generation) with a 16-core NPU. Apple says that M6 has up to four times the AI performance as the M4 Mac mini, double the storage speeds and graphics, and up to 40% faster CPU gains. (Apple seems keenly aware that its core market for the mini is now AI users.) The M5 Pro, on the other hand, can ship with a CPU up to 18 cores and GPU up to 20 cores. You can upgrade the M5 Pro with up to 64GB of RAM, double the maximum memory of the M6.  Whichever Mac mini model you get, Apple says the machine comes with Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and 2.5Gb Ethernet—though you have the option to upgrade to 10Gb Ethernet, as well. You get two USB-C ports in the front with a headphone jack, as well as genlock support via USB-C for better sync between the display and your camera.  The new Mac mini is available to pre-order today. The M6 model starts at $899, while the M5 Pro model starts at $1,699. Both models are now $100 more than their previous-generation counterparts, which isn't surprising, seeing as the global memory crisis is pushing companies to raise prices across the board. Apple itself had already raised prices ahead of this release.Apple's new Mac Studio comes with the new M5 UltraApple's offer for users who want more power out of their Macs is the new Mac Studio. Again, this model looks similar to the previous one, but it's what's inside that's different. The new Mac Studio comes with either Apple's M5 Max or its brand-new M5 Ultra chip. Apple says M5 Max offers 3.9 times faster AI performance than the previous generation, with an 18-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU. The company claims the new Neural Accelerators are now 50% faster than the last Mac Studio, and you can configure it with up to 128GB of RAM. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple says M5 Ultra offers 4.3 times the "peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra." If you're coming from M1 Ultra, Apple says you can expect up to 9.8 times more performance. You can configure a Mac Studio with M5 Ultra with a CPU with up to 36 cores, and a GPU with up to 80 cores, which Apple says is its most powerful graphics processor ever. At launch, you can configure the M5 Ultra with up to 256GB of RAM, but Apple says you'll soon be able to upgrade to 512GB. The Studio has a full array of I/O components, including four Thunderbolt 5 ports, Ethernet, two USB-A ports, HDMI, and a headphone jack. You can connect it with up to eight displays, or up to four Studio Display XDRs.You can pre-order Mac Studios today, starting at $2,499 for the M5 Max model, or $5,499 for the M5 Ultra model. (Though you can certainly pay a lot more if you upgrade the components.) The M5 Max price is technically unchanged, but it is the price Apple increased the Studio line to back in June. The M5 Ultra is now $200 more than it was before. Apple quietly upgraded other products today, tooWhile Apple's official announcements were focused on its two new Mac models and M-series chips, it quietly updated some other products, as well. If you go to buy a new Magic Keyboard from Apple today, you'll notice some of the keys are different, replacing the text with glyphs (e.g., an arrow icon instead of "caps lock" text). While the keyboards are functionally the same, these small updates bring the design in line with Apple's latest laptops. Apple's much-memed "Polishing Cloth" is also changed today, but for the better. While the product itself is the same, it now costs $9, rather than $19. It feels a bit more reasonable to drop it in your cart now, even if it is just a cloth with the Apple logo embossed in the corner.

title: A Bunch of AI Platforms Are Down, Including ChatGPT
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 3, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Robert Way via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok are all experiencing downtime Thursday morning.
                                            OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX AI all confirm issues with their platforms.
                                            It's not clear what the root cause of the issue is at this time, or whether the outages are related.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you had trouble accessing AI platforms Thursday morning, you're not alone. Apps and services, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, were down, or experienced issues with service. ChatGPT and Grok were both unresponsive when I tried to use them, while Claude appeared to respond, at least for me. ChatGPT appears to be experiencing the most issues, at least per Downdetector. The site, which accepts user reports of issues with apps and services, currently shows tens of thousands of reports for ChatGPT alone. Claude and Grok had fewer reports, but still many (thousands) over the course of this morning. According to OpenAI's status page, the company had experienced issues with both ChatGPT and Codex. Anthropic had also acknowledged issues with Claude, including for its Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 models, and said it is working on a fix. SpaceXAI shows that all Grok functions appear to be down at this time. As of 1:19 p.m. ET, all three services now report that they're now up and running. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear exactly what caused these issues, or if they were all related to one another. Typically, outages like these are solved relatively quickly, so it's not a surprise that all three were able to get their systems back by early afternoon. I'll continue to monitor the situation and update this piece accordingly.

title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 1, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Kenneth Cheung / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device, as Mozilla is officially rolling out native ad blocking.
                                            Most ads will be blocked, but users will still see search engine ads and sponsored content from Firefox.
                                            The feature is off by default, so you need to enable it yourself if you want to use it.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Following a slow "experimental" period, Mozilla is now officially rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available in your app. According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox's new feature can block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It can also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list. Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off.

Daniel Oropeza
                            
        
            Daniel Oropeza

            ExperienceDaniel is Lifehacker's Shopping Editor covering tech deals and reviewing TVs, headphones, speakers, and projectors. He earned his master’s in journalism from Columbia University and has reported for the Miami Herald. He lives in Atlanta.

    Table of Contents
    
        
        The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99). That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, according to price-tracking tools, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.
I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.When will Labor Day sales start?Labor Day sales have already started. More retailers are likely to start their own sales leading up to the holiday on Monday, Sept. 7.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Are Labor Day sales worth it?Labor Day has traditionally been a good time to find deals in many categories, but whether they're worth it or not depends entirely on what you're looking for. Compared to sales like Black Friday or Prime Day, Labor Day falls short on volume and quality of discounts, but you might still find a good price on tech or kitchen appliances that will match those holiday prices—or even beat them. (We use price-tracking tools to let you know if a deal is worth it or not.)What other stores have Labor Day sales?Home Depot, Amazon, Wayfair, Target, Walmart, and Best Buy all have Labor Day sales. (Lifehacker will be rounding up deals for all of these sales.)
